title.zh: 长城：两千年的超级工程

clips.send: Dont mix up: Brick didn’t replace earth inside — it wrapped it. The core is still earth and rubble.
clips.text: Dont mix up: Brick didn’t replace earth inside — it wrapped it. The core is still earth and rubble.

clips.send: Han wall. After Emperor Wu’s armies pushed the Xiongnu back, Han built walls and beacon towers through the Hexi Corridor, past Yumen Pass, toward Lop Nur — guarding the new Silk Road.
clips.text: Han wall. After Emperor Wu’s armies pushed the Xiongnu back, Han built walls and beacon towers through the Hexi Corridor, past Yumen Pass, toward Lop Nur — guarding the new Silk Road.

clips.send: The walkway on top. A road for soldiers along the mountains. At Badaling the top is about 5.8 m (19 ft) wide — room for 5 horses or 10 soldiers side by side. Soldiers could move quickly along the wall to wherever the attack came.
clips.text: The walkway on top. A road for soldiers along the mountains. At Badaling the top is about 5.8 m (19 ft) wide — room for 5 horses or 10 soldiers side by side.. Soldiers could move quickly along the wall to wherever the attack came.

clips.send: Hollow watchtower (空心敌台). A fort astride the wall. General Qi Jiguang (戚继光), famous for fighting pirates, had over a thousand hollow towers built on the wall near Beijing. Soldiers lived and stored weapons inside, and shot along the wall from the windows — crossfire against ladders.
clips.text: Hollow watchtower (空心敌台). A fort astride the wall. General Qi Jiguang (戚继光), famous for fighting pirates, had over a thousand hollow towers built on the wall near Beijing.. Soldiers lived and stored weapons inside, and shot along the wall from the windows — crossfire against ladders.

clips.send: Shanhai Pass (山海关). “The First Pass Under Heaven” (天下第一关), where mountains (山) meet the sea (海). At Old Dragon’s Head the wall runs right into the Bohai Sea. In 1644 Qing armies entered the central plains through this pass.
clips.text: Shanhai Pass (山海关). “The First Pass Under Heaven” (天下第一关), where mountains (山) meet the sea (海). At Old Dragon’s Head the wall runs right into the Bohai Sea. In 1644 Qing armies entered the central plains through this pass.

clips.send: Yumen Pass (玉门关, Dunhuang). A Han gateway to the Western Regions. A Tang poem says “the spring wind never crosses Yumen Pass” — it was that remote. Han walls of gravel and reeds still stand nearby.
clips.text: Yumen Pass (玉门关, Dunhuang). A Han gateway to the Western Regions. A Tang poem says “the spring wind never crosses Yumen Pass” — it was that remote. Han walls of gravel and reeds still stand nearby.

clips.send: The land itself. Builders used mountains as part of the defence. Walls follow ridgelines, so attackers must climb a steep slope before they even reach the wall. In the game a ridge adds 2 m of “effective height”. Rivers and cliffs were used too: 2,232.5 km of the Ming line are natural barriers (2009 survey).

clips.send: Qin wall. Qin Shi Huang sent general Meng Tian (蒙恬) north to drive back the Xiongnu (匈奴), then joined and extended the old Qin, Zhao and Yan walls: from Lintao (today’s Min County, Gansu) in the west to Liaodong (in today’s Liaoning) in the east — the “10,000-li Great Wall”.

clips.send: Jilin.
clips.text: Jilin.

clips.send: Dont mix up: The brick wall tourists climb at Badaling is Ming, not Qin. Qin walls were mostly earth and stone.
clips.text: Dont mix up: The brick wall tourists climb at Badaling is Ming, not Qin. Qin walls were mostly earth and stone.

clips.send: Dont mix up: The Great Wall was not built once by one emperor: many dynasties built, joined and rebuilt it over 2,000+ years.
clips.text: Dont mix up: The Great Wall was not built once by one emperor: many dynasties built, joined and rebuilt it over 2,000+ years.

clips.send: Rammed earth (夯土). Soil pounded hard, layer by layer. Wooden boards make a mould; damp soil is poured in and pounded with heavy rammers, about 10–20 cm (4–8 in) per layer. Qin and Han walls are mostly rammed earth or piled stone. Even Ming brick walls often have an earth-and-rubble core inside.
clips.text: Rammed earth (夯土). Soil pounded hard, layer by layer. Wooden boards make a mould; damp soil is poured in and pounded with heavy rammers, about 10–20 cm (4–8 in) per layer.. Qin and Han walls are mostly rammed earth or piled stone. Even Ming brick walls often have an earth-and-rubble core inside.

clips.send: Fired-brick shell. Ming walls wear a brick “coat”. Ming kilns fired huge numbers of bricks; a typical wall brick weighs around 10 kg or more (approx.). Many bricks are stamped with the year and the workshop — an early quality-control system.

clips.send: Jiayu Pass (嘉峪关). The western end of the Ming wall: a fort in the narrow gap between the Qilian Mountains and the Hei Mountains, on the Silk Road. Nicknamed “the mightiest pass under heaven” (天下第一雄关).
clips.text: Jiayu Pass (嘉峪关). The western end of the Ming wall: a fort in the narrow gap between the Qilian Mountains and the Hei Mountains, on the Silk Road. Nicknamed “the mightiest pass under heaven” (天下第一雄关).

clips.send: Crenellations (垛口). Cover for defenders on the outer side. The outer parapet has tall teeth (merlons) with gaps (crenels) to shoot through, plus small holes to look and shoot down. The inner side usually has a lower wall (宇墙) so soldiers don’t fall off.

clips.send: Hushan (虎山, Dandong). On the Yalu River at the border with North Korea — the eastern starting point of the Ming wall according to the 2009 survey.
clips.text: Hushan (虎山, Dandong). On the Yalu River at the border with North Korea — the eastern starting point of the Ming wall according to the 2009 survey.

clips.send: Mutianyu (慕田峪). Watchtowers stand close together on a steep, forested ridge. Parts of the wall have crenellations on both sides, so defenders could fight either way.
clips.text: Mutianyu (慕田峪). Watchtowers stand close together on a steep, forested ridge. Parts of the wall have crenellations on both sides, so defenders could fight either way.

clips.send: Drainage spouts (吐水嘴). Keep rainwater out of the wall. Stone gutters stick out from the wall so rain pours away from the wall face instead of soaking in. Water is the Great Wall’s worst enemy — it freezes, cracks and washes out earth.
clips.text: Drainage spouts (吐水嘴). Keep rainwater out of the wall. Stone gutters stick out from the wall so rain pours away from the wall face instead of soaking in.. Water is the Great Wall’s worst enemy — it freezes, cracks and washes out earth.

clips.send: Warring States walls. Before unification, states walled themselves in — against each other and against nomads from the north. Qi’s wall in Shandong is among the oldest; Chu built a “square wall”; Wei, Zhao, Yan and Qin built walls too.
clips.text: Warring States walls. Before unification, states walled themselves in — against each other and against nomads from the north. Qi’s wall in Shandong is among the oldest; Chu built a “square wall”; Wei, Zhao, Yan and Qin built walls too.

clips.send: Stone foundation. Big cut-stone blocks under Ming walls. Ming builders laid long granite blocks as a base, so the wall would not sink or slide on slopes. Some blocks weigh hundreds of kilograms — carried up mountains by people, donkeys and simple winches.

clips.send: Xinjiang.
clips.text: Xinjiang.

clips.send: Gravel + reed layers. Han builders’ trick in the desert. Near Yumen Pass there is little soil, so Han soldiers alternated gravel with layers of reeds or tamarisk branches. The plant layers bind the gravel. In the dry desert these walls have lasted over 2,000 years.

clips.send: Ming wall. After driving the Mongols north, Ming spent about two centuries building the brick-and-stone wall most visitors see today — from Hushan on the Yalu River to Jiayu Pass: 8,851.8 km including natural barriers (2009 survey).
clips.text: Ming wall. After driving the Mongols north, Ming spent about two centuries building the brick-and-stone wall most visitors see today — from Hushan on the Yalu River to Jiayu Pass: 8,851.8 km including natural barriers (2009 survey).

clips.send: Jin border trenches. The Jurchen Jin dug long ditches backed by earth walls (界壕 jièháo, “border trenches”) across today’s Inner Mongolia and Heilongjiang — against the rising Mongols.
clips.text: Jin border trenches. The Jurchen Jin dug long ditches backed by earth walls (界壕 jièháo, “border trenches”) across today’s Inner Mongolia and Heilongjiang — against the rising Mongols.

clips.send: Badaling (八达岭). Guarding the road to Juyong Pass and Beijing. On average the wall here is about 7.8 m (26 ft) high and 5.8 m (19 ft) wide on top — five horses side by side. It’s the most-visited section.
clips.text: Badaling (八达岭). Guarding the road to Juyong Pass and Beijing. On average the wall here is about 7.8 m (26 ft) high and 5.8 m (19 ft) wide on top — five horses side by side. It’s the most-visited section.

clips.send: Beacon tower (烽火台). The ancient “text message”. Smoke by day, fire by night (白天放烟, 夜间举火): tower to tower, the alarm raced to the rear. Beacon towers often stand on hilltops near or ahead of the wall, where they can see far.

clips.send: Northern Wei – Northern Qi – Sui. Later northern dynasties — Northern Wei, Northern Qi and Sui — kept adding walls in the north.

clips.send: 虎山。今天：辽宁丹东。位于中朝边境的鸭绿江畔，2009年测量认定为明长城的东端起点。

clips.send: 易错点：长城不是某一个皇帝一次修成的，而是两千多年里许多朝代不断修筑、连接和重修的结果。
clips.text: 易错点：长城不是某一个皇帝一次修成的，而是两千多年里许多朝代不断修筑、连接和重修的结果。

clips.send: 空心敌台。骑在城墙上的小堡垒。抗倭名将戚继光调到北方后，主持在北京附近的长城上修建了一千多座空心敌台。士兵可以在里面驻守、储存武器，从窗口向两侧射击，形成交叉火力。

clips.send: 砂砾夹芦苇。汉代在戈壁的筑墙方法。玉门关一带缺少黄土，汉代士兵用砂砾和芦苇（或红柳枝）一层层交替铺筑。植物层把砂砾牢牢“拉”住。在干燥的沙漠里，这样的墙保存了两千多年。

clips.send: 垛口。外侧的齿状掩体。外侧垛墙一高一低，形成垛口，可以瞭望、射击；垛口下方还有射孔。内侧通常是较矮的宇墙，防止士兵跌落。

clips.send: 罗布泊。罗布泊曾是新疆的大咸水湖，如今已干涸成盐碱荒漠。中国第一颗原子弹在这片荒漠中试验成功。

clips.send: 条石基础。明长城墙基多用大条石。明长城用大块条石砌墙基，防止城墙下沉或在山坡上滑动。有的条石重达几百千克，靠人力、牲畜和简单的绞盘运上山。

clips.send: 汉长城。汉武帝派兵打败匈奴后，汉朝在河西走廊修筑长城和烽燧，一直延伸到玉门关以西、罗布泊一带，保护了丝绸之路。

clips.send: 北魏、北齐、隋长城。此后的北魏、北齐、隋等王朝也在北方修筑过长城。

clips.send: 嘉峪关。明长城的西端，位于祁连山和黑山之间的狭窄地带，扼守丝绸之路，号称“天下第一雄关”。

clips.send: 金界壕。女真族建立的金朝在今内蒙古、黑龙江一带挖掘界壕、修筑墙体，防御蒙古。

clips.send: 慕田峪。敌楼密集，建在陡峭的山脊上。部分墙段两侧都有垛口，可以两面御敌。

clips.send: 城砖包砌。明长城的“砖外衣”。明朝烧制了大量城砖，一块城砖一般有十几千克重（约数）。许多城砖上印着烧造年份和窑场名称，出了质量问题可以追查。

clips.send: 明长城。明朝把蒙古势力赶回漠北后，用了约两百年时间修筑长城，东起鸭绿江畔的虎山，西至嘉峪关。2009年测得明长城全长8851.8千米（含天然险）。

clips.send: 烽火台。古代的“快讯”。白天放烟，夜间举火，一座传一座，军情很快传到后方。烽火台常建在城墙内外的山头上，视野开阔。

clips.send: 夯土。一层层夯实的土。用木板夹成模子，倒进湿土，用夯锤反复砸实，每层大约十几厘米厚。秦汉长城多用夯土或石块筑成；明长城的砖墙里面也常常是夯土和碎石。

clips.send: 墙顶马道。山顶上的“公路”。八达岭长城顶宽约5.8米，可容五马并骑、十人并行。士兵可以沿着墙顶迅速赶到受攻击的地方。

clips.send: 地形。“因地形，用险制塞”。长城大多沿着山脊修筑，敌人要先爬上陡坡才能接近城墙。在游戏里，山脊能让城墙的“有效高度”增加2米。河流、悬崖也被利用：明长城中有2232.5千米是天然险（2009年测量）。

clips.send: 玉门关（今敦煌西北）。汉代通往西域的门户。唐诗“春风不度玉门关”写出了它的遥远荒凉。附近至今保存着砂砾夹芦苇筑成的汉长城。

clips.send: 吐水嘴。把雨水排出墙外。石制的排水槽伸出墙外，雨水顺着它流走，不会顺墙渗进去。水是长城最大的“敌人”：渗水、结冰、冲刷都会毁坏城墙。

clips.send: 秦长城。秦始皇派蒙恬北击匈奴，把原来秦、赵、燕三国北部的长城连接起来并加以修筑，西起临洮（今甘肃岷县），东至辽东，号称“万里长城”。

clips.send: 战国长城。统一以前，各诸侯国为了互相防御和抵御北方游牧民族，纷纷修筑长城。山东的齐长城是现存最古老的长城之一；楚国修了“方城”；魏、赵、燕、秦也都修有长城。
